beats.text: It's eighteen forty. You're sitting for your first photo, and you can't move for a full minute.
Blink, and your face turns into a blur.
Early cameras needed up to ninety seconds of light.
But by the eighteen fifties, it took just a few seconds.
So people stayed serious for another reason: a photo was rare, expensive, and forever.
Then came cheap cameras, snapshots, and finally phones.
Today, a photo takes less than a hundredth of a second, and you can smile in all of them.
Their full minute of stillness is your blink.

sources: Early daguerreotype portraits (1839–1845) needed about 60–90 seconds of sitting still; after about 1845 (bromine) exposures fell to a few seconds; serious faces had other reasons too (photos were rare, expensive, solemn). Mental Floss, 'Daguerreotype Q&A'; Getty Museum (2023), 'Say Prunes! The surprising history of the smile in early photographs'.
Modern phone cameras in normal light: exposure times well under 1/100 s (general camera knowledge).
